claim: Neuroligins (NLGNs) are postsynaptic cell adhesion molecules that interact trans-synaptically with neurexins to mediate synapse development and function.
source: Neuroligins (NLGNs) are postsynaptic cell adhesion molecules that interact trans-synaptically with neurexins to mediate synapse development and function.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: NLGN2 is only at inhibitory synapses while NLGN3 is at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: NLGN2 is only at inhibitory synapses while NLGN3 is at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Varoqueaux et al., 2004; Budreck and Scheiffele, 2007; Song et al., 1999) in the introduction.

claim: NLGN3 function at inhibitory synapses in rat CA1 depends on the presence of NLGN2.
source: We found that NLGN3 function at inhibitory synapses in rat CA1 depends on the presence of NLGN2
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that NLGN3 overexpression with NLGN2 knockdown fails to enhance inhibitory responses (Figure 1f and g).

claim: A domain in the extracellular region accounts for the functional difference between NLGN2 and 3 specifically at inhibitory synapses.
source: identified a domain in the extracellular region that accounted for this functional difference between NLGN2 and 3 specifically at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is supported by chimeric construct experiments showing that the NLGN2 extracellular region is necessary for function at inhibitory synapses (Figure 2 and Figure 3).

claim: The presence of a cytoplasmic tail (c-tail) is indispensible for NLGN function at inhibitory synapses.
source: We further show that the presence of a cytoplasmic tail (c-tail) is indispensible
evidence: This is supported by data showing that NLGN2Δ133 truncation mutant fails to enhance inhibitory responses on a reduced endogenous NLGN background (Figure 4e and f).

claim: Two domains in the c-tail are necessary for NLGN function at inhibitory synapses.
source: identified two domains in the c-tail that are necessary for NLGN function at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that mutations at R705 and S714 together impair NLGN function (Figure 7).

claim: A gephyrin-dependent mechanism is disrupted by an autism-associated mutation at R705.
source: These domains point to a gephyrin-dependent mechanism that is disrupted by an autism-associated mutation at R705
evidence: This is supported by data showing that the R705C mutation combined with Y770A (which blocks gephyrin binding) still functions, while R705C combined with S714A does not (Figure 7 and Figure 8).

claim: A gephyrin-independent mechanism is reliant on a putative phosphorylation site at S714.
source: a gephyrin-independent mechanism reliant on a putative phosphorylation site at S714.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that S714A combined with Y770A impairs function, while S714D (phospho-mimic) combined with R705C maintains function (Figure 7 and Figure 8).

claim: Rats express three neuroligins (NLGN1-3).
source: Rats express three neuroligins (NLGN1-3)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: NLGN1 is expressed exclusively at excitatory synapses.
source: NLGN1 is expressed exclusively at excitatory synapses
evidence: This is supported by citations (Varoqueaux et al., 2004; Budreck and Scheiffele, 2007; Song et al., 1999) in the introduction.

claim: NLGN2 is selectively present at inhibitory synapses.
source: NLGN2 is selectively present at inhibitory synapses
evidence: This is supported by citations (Varoqueaux et al., 2004; Budreck and Scheiffele, 2007; Song et al., 1999) in the introduction.

claim: Knockdown of endogenous neuroligins 1–3 reduces inhibitory responses to about 50%.
source: Compared to a previously validated knockdown construct of NLGNs 1–3 (Shipman et al., 2011) which reduces inhibitory synaptic transmission to about 50% (Figure 1a)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a with p=0.0391, n=9.

claim: NLGN2 knockdown alone reduces inhibitory synaptic transmission by 50%.
source: we found that while NLGN2 knockdown alone recapitulated the 50% decrease in inhibitory synaptic transmission (Figure 1b and d)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b with p=0.0002, n=15.

claim: NLGN3 knockdown alone has no effect on inhibitory synaptic transmission.
source: NLGN3 knockdown alone had no effect on inhibitory synaptic transmission (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c with p=0.3013, n=12.

claim: Overexpression of NLGN3 alone enhances inhibitory synaptic transmission.
source: while overexpression of NLGN3 alone does enhance inhibitory synaptic transmission (Figure 1e and g)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e with p=0.0084, n=15.

claim: Overexpression of NLGN3 with a NLGN2 knockdown construct fails to enhance inhibitory responses.
source: overexpression of NLGN3 with a NLGN2 knockdown construct fails to enhance inhibitory responses (Figure 1f and g)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f with p=0.2661, n=12.

claim: NLGN3 overexpression on a NLGN2 knockdown background still enhances excitatory responses similar to NLGN3 overexpression alone.
source: Notably, NLGN3 overexpression on a NLGN2 knockdown background still enhanced excitatory responses similar to NLGN3 overexpression alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c and d)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c and d.

claim: Expression of full-length NLGN2 on a NLGN1-3miR knockdown background results in a large enhancement of inhibitory currents.
source: Expression of the full-length NLGN2 resulted in a large enhancement of inhibitory currents (Figure 2b and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b with p<0.0001, n=25.

claim: A construct containing the NLGN2 extracellular region and NLGN3 cytoplasmic tail enhances inhibitory currents similar to full-length NLGN2.
source: Expression of a construct containing the NLGN2 extracellular region and NLGN3 cytoplasmic tail enhanced inhibitory currents (Figure 2c and e) similar to full-length NLGN2 (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c with p=0.002, n=10.

claim: A construct containing the NLGN3 extracellular region and NLGN2 intracellular region fails to enhance inhibitory currents.
source: expression of a construct containing the NLGN3 extracellular region and NLGN2 intracellular region failed to enhance inhibitory currents (Figure 2d and e)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d with p=0.5771, n=11.

claim: The functional difference between NLGN2 and 3 at inhibitory synapses resides in the extracellular region.
source: suggesting that the functional difference between NLGN2 and 3 at inhibitory synapses resides in the extracellular region.
evidence: This is inferred from the chimeric construct experiments showing that the NLGN2 extracellular region is necessary for function (Figure 2).

claim: The NLGN3 extracellular-NLGN2 intracellular chimeric construct is still able to potentiate excitatory responses.
source: while the NLGN3 extracellular-NLGN2 intracellular chimeric construct failed to enhance inhibitory responses, it was still able to potentiate excitatory responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with p=0.0098, n=10.

claim: There are differential requirements for NLGN3 function at inhibitory versus excitatory synapses.
source: It further shows that there are differential requirements for NLGN3 function at inhibitory versus excitatory synapses
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NLGN3e-2ctail fails at inhibitory but succeeds at excitatory synapses.

claim: The NLGN2 c-tail is capable of functioning at excitatory synapses.
source: and that the NLGN2 c-tail is capable of functioning at excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NLGN3e-2ctail enhances excitatory responses.

claim: Critical dimerization residues are conserved between NLGN2 and 3.
source: the critical dimerization residues, are conserved between NLGN2 and 3, suggesting that differences between NLGN2 and 3 may not be due to differences in ability to dimerize (Dean et al., 2003; Ko et al., 2009; Shipman and Nicoll, 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and sequence analysis.

claim: Splice site A is important for neurexin binding.
source: One notable domain of interest resides in splice site A, which is important for neurexin binding (Ichtchenko et al., 1996; Chih et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There are many differences between NLGN2 and 3 at splice site A.
source: Interestingly, there are many differences between NLGN2 and 3 at this splice site
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Adding NLGN2 onto the NLGN3 extracellular region up to the 623rd residue fails to enhance IPSCs.
source: Neither this chimeric construct (Figure 3b and h) nor one adding back NLGN2 right before splice site A at the 180th amino acid (Figure 3c and h) was able to enhance inhibitory currents.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b with p=0.4229, n=16.

claim: Adding NLGN2 up to the 180th residue fails to enhance IPSCs.
source: Neither this chimeric construct (Figure 3b and h) nor one adding back NLGN2 right before splice site A at the 180th amino acid (Figure 3c and h) was able to enhance inhibitory currents.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c with p=0.2754, n=10.

claim: Adding NLGN2 up to the 52nd residue is successful at conferring NLGN function at inhibitory synapses.
source: However, adding back NLGN2 up to the 52nd amino acid was able to potentiate inhibitory currents (Figure 3d and h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d with p=0.002, n=10.

claim: The domain between residue 52–180 on NLGN2 is sufficient to confer the ability to enhance IPSCs to NLGN3.
source: Further refinement showed that transplanting just the domain between the 52nd and 180th amino acid of NLGN2 was able to fully confer NLGN2 ability to potentiate inhibitory currents onto NLGN3 (Figure 3e and h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e with p=0.0039, n=9.

claim: A chimeric construct containing the uncharacterized extracellular domain of NLGN2 between amino acids 52–164 shows modest enhancement of inhibitory currents.
source: While expression of a chimeric construct containing the uncharacterized extracellular domain of NLGN2 between amino acids 52–164 showed a modest enhancement of inhibitory currents (Figure 3f and h), it was far less than the effect of the full length NLGN2 (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f with p=0.0098, n=10.

claim: A chimera containing only the splice site A domain of NLGN2 fails to enhance inhibitory responses.
source: A chimera containing only the splice site A domain of NLGN2 (Figure 3g and h) failed to enhance inhibitory responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g with p=0.0522, n=12.

claim: The splice site A domain alone does not account for the differences between NLGN2 and 3 function.
source: Together, this suggests that the splice site A domain alone does not account for the differences between NLGN2 and 3 function but that a previously uncharacterized adjacent domain is also required.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that splice site A alone is insufficient (Figure 3).

claim: Full-length NLGN1 is unable to enhance inhibitory responses on a reduced endogenous NLGN background.
source: full-length NLGN1 was unable to enhance inhibitory responses (Figure 4b and d)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b with p=0.6726, n=19.

claim: A chimeric construct containing the NLGN2 extracellular region with a NLGN1 intracellular region is able to enhance inhibitory currents.
source: while a chimeric construct containing the NLGN2 extracellular region with a NLGN1 intracellular region was able to enhance inhibitory currents (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c with p=0.0244, n=11.

claim: Expression of NLGN2Δ133 truncation mutant on a reduced endogenous NLGN background shows no potentiation.
source: expression on a reduced endogenous NLGN background showed no potentiation (Figure 4e and f), indicating that a c-tail is required for proper NLGN function
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e with p=0.6387, n=15.

claim: Overexpression of NLGN2Δ133 truncation mutant on a wild-type background enhances inhibitory currents to a similar extent as full-length NLGN2.
source: While overexpression of this truncation mutant on a wild-type background (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c) enhanced inhibitory currents to a similar extent as full-length NLGN2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and c)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of the c-tail truncation is not due to impaired surface trafficking.
source: Importantly, the effect of the c-tail truncation was not due to impaired surface trafficking as shown by surface immunostaining of the HA-tagged NLGN2 constructs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d and e).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d and e with p=0.189, n=11 cells per group.

claim: Deleting the PDZ domain does not alter the function of NLGN2.
source: We found that deleting the PDZ domain did not alter the function of NLGN2 (Figure 5a and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a with p=0.0098, n=11.

claim: Excision of the proline-rich region still results in significant potentiation of inhibitory currents.
source: However, excision of this domain (NLGN2Δ32–39) or truncation of this domain and everything downstream of it including the PDZ domain (NLGN2Δ39) still resulted in significant potentiation of inhibitory currents (Figure 5b and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b with p=0.0017, n=14 for NLGN2Δ39 and p=0.002, n=10 for NLGN2Δ32–39.

claim: Truncation of all regions downstream of the gephyrin binding domain still potentiates inhibitory currents.
source: truncation of the gephyrin-binding domain and everything downstream of it, including all known functional domains of the NLGN2 c-tail (NLGN2Δ69), all still displayed significant potentiation of inhibitory currents (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c with p=0.0017, n=18.

claim: Expression of NLGN2 with a phospho-mimic mutation Y770A that disrupts gephyrin binding still potentiates inhibitory currents.
source: we found that expression of NLGN2 with a phospho-mimic mutation previously shown to disrupt gephyrin binding (NLGN2 Y770A) (Poulopoulos et al., 2009; Giannone et al., 2013), excision of the whole gephyrin-binding domain (NLGN2Δ55–69), or, most dramatically, truncation of the gephyrin-binding domain and everything downstream of it, including all known functional domains of the NLGN2 c-tail (NLGN2Δ69), all still displayed significant potentiation of inhibitory currents (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d with p=0.0005, n=17 for NLGN2 Y770A.

claim: Excision of the gephyrin-binding domain still results in significant potentiation of inhibitory currents.
source: excision of the whole gephyrin-binding domain (NLGN2Δ55–69), or, most dramatically, truncation of the gephyrin-binding domain and everything downstream of it, including all known functional domains of the NLGN2 c-tail (NLGN2Δ69), all still displayed significant potentiation of inhibitory currents (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d with p=0.0273, n=10 for NLGN2Δ55–69.

claim: Gephyrin knockdown reduces inhibitory currents to about 50%.
source: Expression of this construct reduced inhibitory currents to about 50%, similar to knockdown of all endogenous NLGNs (Figure 6a and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a with p=0.0156, n=8.

claim: NLGN2Δ69 coexpressed with gephyrin and endogenous NLGN knockdown constructs is fully capable of enhancing inhibitory currents.
source: Surprisingly, a NLGN2 truncation mutant lacking all known functional domains of the c-tail (NLGN2Δ69) coexpressed with our gephyrin and endogenous NLGN knockdown constructs was fully capable of enhancing inhibitory currents (Figure 6b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b with p=0.0039, n=9.

claim: NLGN2 can function independently of gephyrin.
source: These results indicate that NLGN2 can function, not only without previously known domains, but entirely independently of gephyrin as well.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NLGN2Δ69 functions even with gephyrin knockdown (Figure 6).

claim: Deletion of a 35 amino acid stretch from NLGN2Δ98–133 results in the loss of enhancement of inhibitory responses.
source: We made further truncations starting at the region closest to our most terminal c-tail truncation (NLGN2Δ133) and found that deletion of a 35 amino acid stretch from that point (NLGN2Δ98–133) resulted in the loss of enhancement of inhibitory responses (Figure 7a and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a with p=0.1698, n=17.

claim: Deletion of a domain of 16 amino acids (NLGN2Δ117–133) shows no enhancement of inhibitory responses.
source: Further refinement identified a domain of 16 amino acids that, when deleted (NLGN2Δ117–133), also showed no enhancement (Figure 7b and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b with p=0.6953, n=10.

claim: Individual mutation at S714A (phospho-null) still enhances inhibitory responses comparable to full-length NLGN2.
source: Individual mutations at these sites, either by expressing the phospho-null (NLGN2-S714A) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a and d), phospho-mimic (NLGN2-S714D) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b and d), or the analogous autism point mutation (NLGN2-R705C) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c and d), still enhanced inhibitory responses comparable to full-length NLGN2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a with p=0.0195, n=9.

claim: Individual mutation at S714D (phospho-mimic) still enhances inhibitory responses comparable to full-length NLGN2.
source: Individual mutations at these sites, either by expressing the phospho-null (NLGN2-S714A) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a and d), phospho-mimic (NLGN2-S714D) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b and d), or the analogous autism point mutation (NLGN2-R705C) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c and d), still enhanced inhibitory responses comparable to full-length NLGN2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b with p=0.0007, n=13.

claim: Individual mutation at R705C (autism mutation) still enhances inhibitory responses comparable to full-length NLGN2.
source: Individual mutations at these sites, either by expressing the phospho-null (NLGN2-S714A) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a and d), phospho-mimic (NLGN2-S714D) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b and d), or the analogous autism point mutation (NLGN2-R705C) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c and d), still enhanced inhibitory responses comparable to full-length NLGN2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1c with p=0.0391, n=9.

claim: The double point mutant NLGN2-R705C-S714A shows dramatically reduced enhancement of inhibitory responses.
source: However, when we expressed the double point mutant of the autism-associated mutation with the phospho-null mutation (NLGN2-R705C-S714A) (Figure 7c and e) the enhancement was dramatically reduced
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c with p=0.0522, n=12.

claim: The double point mutant NLGN2-R705C-S714D shows robust enhancement of inhibitory currents.
source: Notably, when we tested another double point mutant with a phospho-mimic mutation at S714 instead, (NLGN2-R705C-S714D) (Figure 7d and e), we still saw robust enhancement of inhibitory currents
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d with p=0.0002, n=15.

claim: The effect of NLGN2-R705C-S714A is phosphorylation-dependent.
source: showing that our effect is phosphorylation-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between S714A and S714D double mutants with R705C.

claim: The double mutant NLGN2-R705C-Y770A exhibits enhancement comparable to full-length NLGN2.
source: The combined autism mutation and gephyrin-binding double point mutant (NLGN2-R705C-Y770A) exhibited enhancement comparable to full-length NLGN2 (Figure 7f and h)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7f with p=0.0005, n=17.

claim: The double mutant NLGN2-S714A-Y770A shows significantly reduced enhancement of inhibitory responses.
source: while the combined phospho-null mutation and gephyrin-binding double point mutant (NLGN2-S714A-Y770A) showed significantly reduced enhancement (Figure 7g and h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7g with p=0.0274, n=13.

claim: There are two pathways for NLGN function at inhibitory synapses: a gephyrin-independent pathway modulated at S714 and a gephyrin-dependent pathway modulated at both R705 and Y770.
source: Together, we propose the existence of two pathways: a gephyrin-independent pathway modulated at S714 and a gephyrin-dependent pathway modulated at both R705 and Y770 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of results with double mutants (Figure 7 and Figure 8).

claim: Proper balance between inhibitory and excitatory connections is important for proper functioning of neuronal circuits.
source: Proper balance between inhibitory and excitatory connections is important for proper functioning of neuronal circuits (Maćkowiak et al., 2014; Bang and Owczarek, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cell adhesion molecules have a critical role in coordinating the apposition of presynaptic terminals with postsynaptic sites of differentiation.
source: Cell adhesion molecules have a critical role in coordinating the apposition of presynaptic terminals with postsynaptic sites of differentiation (Washbourne et al., 2004; Yamagata et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Less is known about how cell adhesion molecules are organized at inhibitory synapses compared to excitatory synapses.
source: While much work has been done to determine the molecular organization of cell adhesion molecules at excitatory synapses, less is known about how these components are organized at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field.

claim: NLGN2 and 3 share many previously identified domains both in their extracellular and intracellular regions.
source: NLGN2 and 3 share many previously identified domains both in their extracellular and intracellular regions.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and previous literature.

claim: It is currently unknown whether NLGN2 and 3 perform the same function at inhibitory synapses.
source: Despite the similarities between the two proteins, it is currently unknown whether they perform the same function at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Splice site A has been proposed to affect NLGN binding to its presynaptic neurexin partner.
source: One notable difference between NLGN2 and 3 resides in the extracellular region at splice site A which has previously been proposed to affect NLGN binding to its presynaptic neurexin partner (Ichtchenko et al., 1996; Chih et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NLGN2 functions through a direct interaction on its cytoplasmic tail with gephyrin.
source: It has been suggested that NLGN2 functions through a direct interaction on its cytoplasmic tail with gephyrin, a scaffold protein thought to be essential for stabilizing glycine and GABAA receptors at inhibitory synapses (Choii and Ko, 2015; Tyagarajan and Fritschy, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Gephyrin is a scaffold protein thought to be essential for stabilizing glycine and GABAA receptors at inhibitory synapses.
source: gephyrin, a scaffold protein thought to be essential for stabilizing glycine and GABAA receptors at inhibitory synapses (Choii and Ko, 2015; Tyagarajan and Fritschy, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Collybistin is a brain-specific guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) that helps regulate the localization of gephyrin.
source: In addition, it has been proposed that collybistin, a brain-specific guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF), helps regulate the localization of gephyrin, and that NLGN2 is a specific activator of collybistin via a direct interaction at the proline rich region in its cytoplasmic tail (Kins et al., 2000; Poulopoulos et al., 2009; Soykan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NLGN2 is a specific activator of collybistin via a direct interaction at the proline rich region in its cytoplasmic tail.
source: NLGN2 is a specific activator of collybistin via a direct interaction at the proline rich region in its cytoplasmic tail (Kins et al., 2000; Poulopoulos et al., 2009; Soykan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There has been no direct study of whether interactions between NLGN2 and gephyrin/collybistin are necessary for proper functioning of NLGNs at inhibitory synapses.
source: While previous studies have been able to link these interactions to NLGN2, there has been no direct study of whether these interactions are necessary for proper functioning of NLGNs at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: NLGN2 is a critical component of inhibitory synapses.
source: We found that NLGN2 is a critical component of inhibitory synapses
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that NLGN2 knockdown reduces inhibitory transmission (Figure 1).

claim: The extracellular region is important for specifying function at a particular synapse while the intracellular region is important for carrying out the molecular mechanisms.
source: Our work highlights unique and separate roles for the extracellular and intracellular regions in specifying and carrying out NLGN function respectively.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results presented.

claim: NLGN2 knockout animals specifically display a deficit in PV but not SOM inputs onto hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: Previous work using simultaneous recording from connected neurons showed that NLGN2 knockout animals specifically displayed a deficit in PV but not SOM inputs onto hippocampal pyramidal neurons (Gibson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: NLGN3 knockout animals show an enhancement of CCK inputs but no change in PV inputs.
source: A similar set of studies in NLGN3 knockout animals showed an enhancement of CCK inputs but no change in PV inputs (Földy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The majority of NLGN3 is not localized synaptically while the majority of NLGN2 is synaptically located in cerebral cortical neurons.
source: Previous work looking at overexpression of NLGN2 or 3 in cerebral cortical neurons noticed that the majority of NLGN3 was not localized synaptically while the majority of NLGN2 was synaptically located (Fekete et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: There is a readily available pool of NLGN3 located outside the synapse that could be recruited in response to induction of plasticity.
source: From this, we can surmise the presence of a readily available pool of NLGN3 located outside the synapse that could be recruited and associate with NLGN2 in response to induction of plasticity.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on previous observations.

claim: Different neurexin isoforms are expressed at different types of synapses.
source: Previous work has already shown that different neurexin isoforms are expressed at different types of synapses, and that the neurexin isoform expressed at inhibitory synapses can bind to NLGN2 but not NLGN1 (Fuccillo et al., 2015; Futai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The neurexin isoform expressed at inhibitory synapses can bind to NLGN2 but not NLGN1.
source: the neurexin isoform expressed at inhibitory synapses can bind to NLGN2 but not NLGN1 (Fuccillo et al., 2015; Futai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NLGN3 needs to associate with NLGN2 in order to bind to the neurexins at an inhibitory synapse.
source: Thus, it is possible that NLGN3, which seems to be able to bind to the neurexins at excitatory synapses by itself, needs to associate with NLGN2 in order to bind to the neurexins at an inhibitory synapse
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on experimental results.

claim: A special property of NLGN2 that enables NLGN3 to function at inhibitory synapses resides in a unique domain in its extracellular region.
source: and this special property of NLGN2 resides in a unique domain in its extracellular region that we have now identified.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results with chimeric constructs.

claim: NMDA receptors are able to bind to the extracellular region of NLGN1 but not NLGN2 or 3.
source: Previous work has shown that NMDA receptors are able to bind to the extracellular region of NLGN1 but not NLGN2 or 3 (Budreck et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The presence of the B splice site insertion in NLGN1 enables it to enhance NMDA currents and promote LTP.
source: In addition, the presence of the B splice site insertion in NLGN1 enables it to enhance NMDA currents and promote LTP, and this site is notably absent in NLGN3 (Shipman and Nicoll, 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: MAM domain-containing glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor proteins (MDGAs) are able to negatively regulate the function of NLGN2 through an interaction within their extracellular region.
source: previous work has shown that MAM domain-containing glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor proteins (MDGAs) are able to negatively regulate the function of NLGN2 through an interaction within their extracellular region (Pettem et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Glycosylation state can affect neurexin binding to neuroligins.
source: Also, there are multiple glycosylation sites in the extracellular region of the NLGNs and previous work has shown that glycosylation state can affect neurexin binding (Comoletti et al., 2003; Hoffman et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Any NLGN c-tail is able to function at inhibitory synapses if linked with a NLGN2 extracellular region.
source: Our results with chimeric constructs show that any NLGN c-tail is able to function at inhibitory synapses if linked with a NLGN2 extracellular region
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with chimeric constructs (Figure 4).

claim: The NLGN2 c-tail is able to function at excitatory synapses when linked with the NLGN3 extracellular region.
source: and that the NLGN2 c-tail is able to function at excitatory synapses when linked with the NLGN3 extracellular region.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing NLGN3e-2ctail enhances EPSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: There is no specificity within the c-tail itself to determine NLGN function at either an excitatory or inhibitory synapse.
source: This suggests that there is no specificity within the c-tail itself to determine NLGN function at either an excitatory or inhibitory synapse.
evidence: This is inferred from the interchangeability of c-tails in chimeric constructs.

claim: Overexpression of chimeric constructs containing NLGN1 extracellular linked to NLGN2 intracellular, or NLGN2 extracellular linked to NLGN1 intracellular, is fully capable of enhancing excitatory and inhibitory currents respectively.
source: These results are consistent with previous work showing that overexpression on a wild-type background of chimeric constructs containing NLGN1 extracellular linked to NLGN2 intracellular, or NLGN2 extracellular linked to NLGN1 intracellular, is fully capable of enhancing excitatory and inhibitory currents respectively (Futai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The particular type of synapse determines which residues in the c-tail will be utilized.
source: While the c-tail is the toolbox that contains all the functional residues necessary to perform at either an excitatory or inhibitory synapse, it is important to note that the particular type of synapse determines which residues will be utilized.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential requirements at excitatory vs inhibitory synapses.

claim: Phosphorylation at the gephyrin binding domain enables preferential recruitment of PSD-95 versus gephyrin to the intracellular region of NLGN1.
